To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 2 imprecise p values out of 13 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p < .05 The interacting sibling pairs showed significantly higher brain synchrony than randomly permuted non-sibling pairs in 19 ROIs (FDR-corrected p < .05).
p < .05 Synchrony in frontal and temporal regions was weakly modulated by cooperative and competitive sibling relationship characteristics; however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously (uncorr. p < .05).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 10 distinct packages/libraries: glob, matplotlib, nilearn, numpy, os, pandas, random, scipy, seaborn, statsmodels. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No list of the Python packages the code needs (a requirements.txt, environment.yml, Pipfile.lock, poetry.lock, uv.lock or pyproject.toml) was found anywhere in the repository. Without one, the package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and they may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing a requirements.txt that lists each package with its version (for example the output of pip freeze).

Careless Responding

31 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, 16 were flagged only by short-scale straightlining (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

What this does not cover. Only 1 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script uses a location that exists only on your computer.

  • hyperscanning_CoTT_final.ipynb reads /path/to/data/social_atlas.xlsx.

No other computer has that folder, and the file is also not in the deposit.

  1. Add the file to the deposit.
  2. In the script, write the location from the top folder of your project, such as data/survey.csv. In R, here::here(“data”, “survey.csv”) does this for you.
  3. Remove any setwd() lines.

This module also assesses whether the paper’s Python code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 1 Python code file.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no source()-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an import loads a module, not the paper’s own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

SPSS data

SPSS data and syntax (.sav + .sps) are present. This module does not execute SPSS syntax itself — the syntax is at least documented, but not run here. If an SPSS-Viewer file (.spv) is also deposited, its results are extracted directly (no execution needed); consider adding one if not. Consider depositing the analysis in jamovi (.omv) or JASP (.jasp) instead: these formats store the data and the analyses together in one file, so the results are reproducible from the file itself.

Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

1 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook file bundles the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the file itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 10 result tables (37 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Although the single-brain approach has considerably advanced our knowledge of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying social cognition, a major limitation is that participants are not actively involved in real-time social interactions (Czeszumski et al., 2022; Schilbach & Redcay, 2025).

To confirm this latter criterion, participants were screened using the short version of the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID IV; Wittchen et al., 1997).

Participants were then interviewed by a psychologist, if necessary, to verify their suitability for the study.

Participants were recruited through flyers in university buildings and social media platforms.

After voluntary written informed consent was obtained, participants received verbal instructions about the study and task instructions using pre-recorded videos to ensure consistency of instructions across pairs.

Participants were not allowed to communicate during the task instructions in order to prevent any prior coordination.

Following the scanner session, participants completed self-report questionnaires using the “Sosci survey” online platform (https://www.soscisurvey.de/).

Participants completed all blocks in the same order, as preregistered.

It is possible that during easy blocks, participants were similarly thinking about their partner’s intentions and actions.

Two participants are simultaneously scanned, and task activity is synchronized through a server.

Ethics approval statement:

The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee of the Medical Faculty of RWTH Aachen University (EK 407/20).

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Meta-scientific research has shown that deviations from preregistrations are often not reported or checked, and that the most common deviations concern the sample size. We recommend manually checking the full preregistration at the link above, and have provided the preregistered sample size.

5jbk8 The sample size will be about 40 sibling pairs (80 participants). The final sample will be determined by the time for the study and the financial support.
The previous study is planned to recruit 20 pairs for the behavioral pilot study to test all the tasks (we have already measured 14 of the 20 pairs).

research_questions Overall aim: to investigate the neural underpinnings of intra- and inter- brain activity during sibling interactions, specifically during cooperative, competitive, dominant, and aggressive behavior.

Cooperative task (CoTT):
1. Validation: We expect that pairs with higher INS will perform better (described as deleting more lines) in the CoTT task. Moreover, we expect that participants will have higher INS during easy compared to complex trials.
2. Group comparison: We expect cooperative pairs to perform better and have higher INS than competitive pairs.
3. Leadership: We expect that leader-follower pairs will perform better and have higher INS than follower-follower pairs.
*Leader participant is defined as the participant who makes the first moves more frequently (indicating the direction he/she wants to take).
4. Feedback: We expect that positive feedback will increase INS in the consecutive block.
5. Intra-brain activity: Based on the previous literature we expect to find some activations in frontal and temporal cortices, in areas such as precunei, PFC, ACC, superior/middle temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, caudate, or supplementary motor area.
6. Inter-brain activity (INS): based on the previous literature, we expect to find higher INS in TPJ, and the PFC.

Dominant task (ICG):
1. Validation: We expect that pairs with higher INS will perform better (finish with a higher pair outcome).
2. Group comparison: We expect higher INS in cooperative pairs than competitive pairs.
3. Behavior level: Assuming that there will be differences in dominance behavior observable in siblings’ interaction, we expect to find the following: 1) More cooperative pairs will a) have fewer crashes and b) smaller difference in their number of winning trials; 2) dominate-subordinate pairs will a) have less crashes and b) a larger differences in their number of winning trials, with the dominant sibling winning more; 3) dominant-dominant pairs will have a) more crashes and b) a smaller difference in their number of winning trials.
4. Intra-brain activity: We expect to find higher activity during the competition (mutual-defection) than cooperative behavior in DLPFC, OFC, and temporal cortices.
5. Inter-brain activity: We expect to find higher and denser synchronization (more inter-brain connections) in cooperation (mutual-cooperation and tit-for-tat) trials than in defection trials. Based on the previous literature, this higher INS might be located in frontal areas such as OFC, frontopolar cortex (BA 10), superior frontal gyrus, cingulate motor area, precuneus/superior parietal lobule (BA 7), and TPJ. We also expect to find high INS in TPJ in dominant-subordinate pairs and that the direction of the synchronization goes from the dominant to the subordinate.
6. We expect that subordinate individuals will describe their strategy in cooperative or fair terms while dominant individuals will describe their strategy in competition, dominance, or aggression terms (assessed by self-report questions at the end of the task).
7. Questionnaires: We expect that more competitive individuals will show higher scores on the conflict and rivalry factors in the Adult Sibling Relationship Questionnaire, as well as higher scores on the Dominance, Prestige, and Leadership Scale, the Personal Development Competitive Attitude Scale, the Hypercompetitive Attitude Scale, the Personal Sense of Power Scale and on dominant leadership and ruthless self-advancement factors in the Rank Style Peers Questionnaire.
8. Gender: We expect brothers to show more dominant behavior than sisters. Since sex studies differ in their results, we refrain from a specific hypothesis concerning the brain area, but expect potential differences in the locations of INS characterizing male-male and female-female pairs.

Aggressive task (iTAP):
In this task we have two aims:
a) To analyze the aggressive behavior.
1. We expect that non-aggressive pairs will have higher synchrony than aggressive pairs.
2. Intra-brain activity: We expect to find the commonly reported areas during the classic TAP such as PFC, OFC, ACC, thalamus, amygdala, and insula (although there may be differences because 1) participants are having a real interaction 2) participants know each other well).
3. Inter-brain activity: To our knowledge, this is the first time that purely aggressive behavior will be studied using the hyperscanning technique. Based on single-person results, we might find higher INS between both non-aggressive and aggressive-aggressive pairs in different areas relevant to process the reaction to provocation and aggression (PFC, OFC, ACC, thalamus, amygdala, and insula and others, important to understand the actions of another individual such as TPJ).
4. Gender: We expect brothers to show more aggressive behavior than sisters. Since sex studies differ in their results, we cannot make a specific hypothesis in the brain area but expect a different INS between male-male and female-female, perhaps located in different areas.

b) Side aim: Exploring the mentalizing behavior through the rock, paper, and scissors game.

1. Intra-brain activity: Based on the previous literature, we expect to find activation in mentalizing areas such as PFC, anterior paracingulate cortex, precuneus, TPJ, insula, or superior/middle temporal gyrus. We also expect to find different activations related to different outcomes (win, lose and tie), as well as whether the participant sticks to their previous selection or changes their decision (e.g., in the STG or insula).
2. Inter-brain activity: We expect to find activation in ToM areas such as PFC, precuneus, ACC, TPJ. If we find increased INS, we expect that higher INS during the decision phase will be associated with higher INS during the outcome phase. We expect to find increased INS during win feedback.
study_type Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
blinding No blinding is involved in this study.
study_design_overview The protocol of the pilot study can be found here: DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/QDEVJ

The study includes same-sex sibling pairs, with a maximum of 5 years between them and an age range from 18 to 35 years old. These pairs will be classified into two groups using the Siblings Type Questionnaire (STQ, Stewart 2001). The first group will be defined as cooperative, supportive, and intimate relationships (high mutuality, and low criticism, apathy, competition subscales), and the second group will be characterized by more conflictual, competitive, hostile, and apathetic relationships (presenting the opposite pattern in the STQ subscales).
Sibling pairs will be measured on the same day once at the same time.

Experimental procedure
The procedure of the hyperscanning study will be carried out as follows: at the beginning of the experiment, participants will be informed about the study and all relevant procedures. We start with instructions about the study and the tasks. Subsequently, a one-hour MRI session will follow, including an initial localizer, and structural T1-weighted image acquisition. Later, they will receive further task-related instructions, and when all is understood, upon which they will be asked to complete all three computer-based tasks while a T2-weighted image is being acquired. Then, there will be a 10 minutes break. Afterward, individuals will be asked to complete several questionnaires (See Figure Time structure.png, ). Lastly, all participants will be compensated. In general, it is estimated that the experiment will last about three hours.

Tasks designs:

Cooperation task design:
The Cooperation Tetris Task (CoTT), is a cooperative game, using the well-known Tetris game. In the original game, a descending piece must be fitted to a structure of pieces at the bottom of the playing field. During fall, the piece can be (1) moved (left / right) and (2) rotated to fit. The player wins points every time they completely filled a line with pieces. To make this game interactive, we modified the original version into a two-player scenario. Here, one player can only move and the other can only rotate the piece, which switches every block. Thus, only with the coordination and cooperation of both players is it possible to get the piece in the right position in order to fill a line. Which player moves or rotates will be selected randomly for the first block and it will switch sequentially in the next blocks. Each block will contain three easy and three complex scenarios. In easy scenarios, there is only one clear position to put the piece, while in complex scenarios there are two equally good positions to place the piece so that it creates a conflict between players. Hence, complex scenarios leave more room for leader-follower behaviors to show. In total, this task has 48 scenarios (192 trials in total), which are divided into 4 blocks. For an example of an easy and complex scenario, see figures 1 and 2 of the file “MRI task.pdf”.

Dominance task design:
As far as we know, there are no specific behavioral tasks for real-time dominance behavior and interactions. Some paradigms have studied how people behave when they are forced to adopt the role of “leader” or “subordinate”, but this behavior does not come naturally. To study a real interaction it is important to let the participants make a decision and depending on that decision they will be classified as dominant or subordinate. In this sense, we suggest that the chicken game, a task that is generally used to study cooperation and competition but taking the definition of dominance written above, can also be used to study dominant and subordinate behavior.
The Interactive Chicken Game (ICG) is a modified version of the chicken’s game. This paradigm, which is part of the game theory, creates a conflict between two players. In the original version, two cars drive towards each other until they collide. Each player is in control of one of the cars, such that they select in a matrix to turn away beforehand and yield the road to the other player. If neither player turns, they crash. This similar defection of both players and results in the worst outcome (Astolfi et al., 2010). If both the players cooperate (if both turn), they do not win any points (or have a small win). If one player turns and the other defects, the defector receives a high reward, while the cooperator receives a high loss. The payoff matrix is not fixed, thus the amount and valence of outcomes have changed across studies (De Heus, Hoogervorst, & Van Dijk, 2010). The players aim to reach the maximum score. In this version to increase interactivity in our task, we have adapted the game showing participants a video of two cars approaching (first-person driver’s perspective). Depending on the moment a player decides to turn, the reward/ loss will be different (the closer to the collision point, the higher the outcome). There is an interval of collision in which, if they cross the line, the car continues forward and a car crash cannot be avoided (defect condition). This point of non-return was set to second 5 and the crash at second 6. After the behavioral pilot test, we decided to add a decision phase consisting of a question about their intuition of what they think they will do in the next game “turn” or “continue”. We tell the participants in the instructions that this has to be a quick and intuitive decision of what they plan to do, but of course, it is not the final decision, and they can change it if they feel so while driving. After that, they see a video of the cars approaching, and finally the feedback phase. This task has a total of 42 trials, divided into three blocks. To see the design of the conditions and each trial see figures 4, 6, and 7 of the file “MRI tasks.pdf”.
In the classic version of this game, there is only a choice to be made between turning vs. continuing (cooperating vs. defecting), which is a binary decision, but we believe that by widening the range of decisions we can see a broader and more complex behavior (if one person is more subordinate and always turns at the beginning if there is a cooperative behavior of always turning at the same point (e.g. point 5), or how the dominant behavior emerges (lengthening the moment of the turn, always crashing, etc.).

Aggressive task design:
The interactive Taylor Aggression Paradigm (iTAP) is a modified version of the TAP (Taylor, 1967). In the original version, participants were told to play against an ostensible opponent in a competitive reaction time task. Participants selected the intensity of an electric shock to administer or the amount of money or points to be subtracted to the ostensible opponent in case he/she loses the trial, who ostensibly did the same for them. If the participant lost the competition round, which was preprogrammed, he/she received a shock of their opponent’s choosing (manipulating the level of provocation). The behavioral response to this provocation served as a measure for reactive aggression.
One of the main modifications in the current study is the introduction of a second real opponent. Because of the introduction of this real second player, we have changed the following aspects:
1) Usually a competition reaction time task is used in the competition phase, but we will use the “rock, paper, and scissors game” since the competition reaction time task is less reliable if we manipulate the win/lose trials. In this well-known game, participants have to select between three options “rock”, “paper” and “scissors”. A player who decides to play rock will beat another player who has chosen scissors, but will lose to one who has played paper; a player who selected paper will lose to a play of scissors. If both participants chose the same option, none of them will win. We will use this condition as a control condition in which the provocation is ineffective.
2) The outcome of the competition task will be pre-selected so all participants will lose, win and tie the same amount of rounds (specifically four wins, four loses, and three ties per block). The outcomes are pseudorandomized and fixed across all participants, and both receive the same outcome each trial.
3) The money subtractions in the current version are actually chosen by the players (in contrast to the pre-selected provocations of a computer-programmed opponent in the original paradigms). The only manipulation that will be made to induce a conflict situation is the manipulation of the first five trials in the second block (both will see that their partner provoked them). We have pre-set the provocation values starting at 30, 50, 50, 60, and 70 cents for all participants (this way everyone will start the block with a medium-high provocation).
4) We include a non-aggressive option because this is one of the main criticisms of the original task (Tedeschi, & Quigley, 1996) so that participants are “forced” to select between the options of the low, medium, or high aggressiveness. However, in our task, there is a non-aggressive option (select 0), which assures us that if the participant chooses a low, medium, or high aggression option, it is done voluntarily and not because they had no other option.
This task consists of 33 trials, divided into three blocks (non-provocation, post-manipulation, recovery blocks). Each block has 11 trials, and between the first and second block, there will be five manipulated trials. To see the design of each trial see figure 8 of the file “MRI tasks.pdf”.
All measurements will be conducted via the clinic’s own 3T scanners. A virtual server is hosted at the Brain Imaging Facility to handle any communication for the hyperscanning platform. Experimental paradigms are synchronized by having the paradigm-presenting computers located at the respective fMRI scanners (hereafter referred to as “client”) communicate with this server over TCP/IP. These clients will send paradigm-relevant information like “readiness” and trial information to the server. Upon receiving specific messages from both clients the server replies to both clients with an appropriate message. Contrary to starting the experimental paradigm based on a scanner trigger, as is common practice, the paradigms will send a trigger signal over a parallel port to start the prepared MRI sequence. This ensures that both scanners are synchronized with a maximum latency of approximately 16 milliseconds. To see how each task is synchronized see figures 2, 5, and 9 from the “MRI task.pdf” file.

randomization The order of the paradigms is fixed for all participants.
In the Cooperative Tetris task, the scenarios have been randomly arranged to each block and will be displayed following always the same order to participants (easy-complex-easy-complex-easy-complex).
In the Interactive Chicken Game, videos will be displayed randomly (simple randomization) throughout the blocks.
In the Interactive TAP, the feedback order has been already randomly arranged and will be shown in the same order for all participants.
existing_data Registration prior to creation of data
data_collection_procedures Inclusion criteria are to be a pair of siblings of the same sex, within an age range of 18-35 years, and a maximum difference of five years between them. All participants have normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
Exclusion criteria: Any neurological abnormalities, psychotic symptoms, mental illness, or substance-related disorders that may impair cognitive function, as well as any MRI contraindications (such as metal in the body, pregnancy, or intrauterine device, among others).
The present study will recruit 40 sibling pairs, all of them will be healthy controls.
Same-sex siblings will be recruited through flyers (containing information about the study, including inclusion and exclusion criteria, study duration, and participation rates). These flyers will be posted in local shops in Aachen (Germany), as well as through Internet forums and social media such as Facebook.
All individuals will receive the same amount of €60 after the experiment.
During the recruitment phase, participants will fill out a recruitment questionnaire with demographic data and the Sibling Type Questionnaire (STQ) followed by oral screening and information procedures.
Participants who do not fit our criteria will be excluded.
Based on the STQ scores, participants will be classified into two groups (cooperative and conflictual siblings). The cooperative group will include pairs with high mutuality, low criticism, low apathy, low competition. The conflictual group will include pairs with the opposite pattern.
sample_size The sample size will be about 40 sibling pairs (80 participants). The final sample will be determined by the time for the study and the financial support.
The previous study is planned to recruit 20 pairs for the behavioral pilot study to test all the tasks (we have already measured 14 of the 20 pairs).
sample_size_rationale Few studies investigated social interaction with the fMRI hyperscanning technique. Based on recent similar studies, the sample sizes range from 17 pairs (Koike et al., 2019), 19 pairs (Abe et al., 2019), 43 pairs (Tomlin, Nedic, Prentice, Holmes, & Cohen, 2013) to 48 pairs (Koike et al., 2016). Since we aim to have a powerful sample, while at the same time including a relatively homogeneous group of healthy participants, we think that, based on the numbers included in prior studies, 40 pairs seem an appropriate size for studying social interaction between siblings with fMRI hyperscanning.
Moreover, the sample size of 40 pairs was also reached because of the availability of funds, time, and recruitment constraints.
stopping_rule We will stop measuring in September 2023 due to time constraints.
manipulated_variables In the cooperative Tetris task, we manipulate the difficulty of trials. The two levels of this variable are easy (1) and complex (2) scenarios.
In the interactive chicken game, there is no active experimental manipulation. The experiment is thus a natural observation of the behavior of each sibling pair.
In the interactive TAP, we manipulate the level of provocation for the first trials of the second block. In the first block the provocation will not be manipulated (we will let them decide the level of punishment), but in the first five trials of the second block, the provocation will be manipulated.
measured_variables In the cooperation Tetris task, cooperative behavior will be measured by the number of deleted lines, as well as leadership behavior, which will be obtained by calculating who makes the first move more often. We will also measure the feedback siblings give to each other by selecting between three statements (positive, neutral, or negative). Moreover, brain activity will be measured using the BOLD signal.
We will measure the individual success (number of deleted lines) per individual and pair. We will also measure the efficiency per individual and pair. Efficiency is defined as the ratio between how many movements the person/partner needed to delete a line and how many were the minimum necessary to accomplish that action. In this way we are not only looking at whether or not they were able to delete a line each trial but how effective they were in doing so. We expect that the more coordinated (and therefore more synchronized) pairs will have both high success and efficiency ratios.
After each block, some questions will be asked to assess personal success, responsibility for overall performance, shared mental representation, leadership, and teamwork. At the end of the task, we will ask them how much they liked the task, how difficult it was, and how often they play Tetris.
In the interactive chicken game, dominance behavior will be measured by the participant’s decisions, which can be to turn or to go ahead (in the intuition question and while driving). Reaction time is defined as the time it takes for participants to press the turn/continue button in the intuition question and when the participant decides to turn while driving will also be measured. We also measure if the participant presses after the point of non-return. After each block, some questions will be asked to assess responsibility for the outcome, personal motivation and to rate how much some statements represent how they felt when they won or lost a trial. In addition, participants will receive feedback on who won, who lost the previous block, or if they tied. Some questions about his/her and his/her sibling’s behavioral intentions and strategy during the game will be asked at the end of the task. Moreover, brain activity will be measured using the BOLD signal.
In the interactive Taylor Aggression Paradigm (iTAP) - aggressive behavior will be measured by the amount of money that participants select to be subtracted from their sibling in the decision phase (from 0 to 90), and the aggression level in trial x serves as the provocation level in trial x + 1 to the other sibling. This interdependence is tested statistically. Furthermore, brain activity will be measured using the BOLD signal.
After each block, some questions will be asked to assess personal motivation, aggressive intentions, fairness emotion, and to rate how much some statements represent how they felt when they won or lost a trial. In addition, participants will receive feedback on who won, who lost the previous block, or if they tied. Some questions about his/her and his/her sibling’s behavioral intentions and strategy during the game will be asked at the end of the task.
Demographics: Participants will report their current age, socio-economic level, level of education, current romantic relationship status, handedness, and some questions about their relationship with their parents during their childhood.
Questionnaires:
1. Sibling Type Questionnaire (STQ; Stewart, 2001): this questionnaire is assessed during the recruitment phase to classify the participants. It is a self-report questionnaire with 50 items that assess mutuality, criticism, apathy, competition, and longing factors in a sibling relationship.
2. Aggression Questionnaire (AG; Buss, & Perry, 1992): 29-items scale based on the ranking of statements along a 5-point continuum from “extremely uncharacteristic of me” to “extremely characteristic of me”, yielding 4 factors: Physical Aggression, Verbal Aggression, Anger, and Hostility.
3. Adult Sibling Relationship Questionnaire (ASRQ; Stocker, Lanthier, & Furman, 1997): 81-items scale spread over 14 subscales that assess the qualitative features of sibling relationships in adults.
4. Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11; Patton, Stanford, & Barratt, 1995): 30-items on a 4-point scale that assesses impulsive behaviors and preferences.
5. Dominance, prestige, and leadership scale (DoPL; Suessenbach, Loughnan, Schönbrodt, Moore, & Back, 2019): 18-items on a 6-point scale that assesses social power motives, specifically desires for dominance, prestige, and leadership.
6. Personal Development Competitive Attitude Scale (PDCA; Ryckman, Hammer, Kaczor, & Gold, 1996): the 15-items scale that assesses the desire to improve our own personal performance or “competing to excel”.
7. Hypercompetitive Attitude Scale (HCA; Ryckman, Hammer, Kaczor, & Gold, 1990): the 26-items scale that assesses the desire to have a better performance than the other, or “competing to win”.
8. Machiavellianism Scale (Mach IV; Christie, & Geis, 1970): 20-items self-report measure of Machiavellianism.
9. State-Trait Anger Expression Inventory (STAXI; Spielberger, 2010): the 57-items scale that assesses the intensity of anger as an emotional state (State Anger) and the disposition to experience angry feelings as a personality trait (Trait Anger).
10. Rank Style with Peers Questionnaire (RSPQ; Zuroff, Fournier, Patall, & Leybman, 2010): 17-items scale subdivided into 3 subscales that assess the interaction style people typically use to maintain or improve social standing among peers.
11. Personal Sense of Power scale (Anderson, John, & Keltner, 2012): 8-items on a 7-points scale that assesses the personal sense of power in a given relationship.
12. NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI; McCrae, & Costa Jr, 2004): the 60-items scale that evaluates personality traits divided into subcategories such as Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness.
indices For the CoTT, we will take the average cooperative performance per block and across the entire task (defined as the number of deleted lines) to create a single measure of cooperative behavior per block and sibling pair.
For the other tasks, we will first model the behavior trial-by trial on the individual level and the dual (sibling) level. As the individual responses within the dyad are unlikely to be independent but influenced by the characteristics of the other member, interdependence between the individual responses is assumed (which prevents significance bias). Since commonly used statistical procedures assume independent observations, and we cannot assume this independence, it is necessary to treat the dyad rather than the individual as the unit of the analysis. The Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM: Kashy & Kenny, 1999; Kenny, 1996) is designed to measure interdependence within interpersonal relationships because takes into account interdependencies by measuring associations between scores within the dyad and assessing the extent to which each member of the dyad influences the responses of the other member (Fitzpatrick, Gareau, Lafontaine, & Gaudreau, 2016). In this model, individual measures are treated as being nested within the dyad.
statistical_tests Overall, statistical analyses will be performed using IBM SPSS Statistics Version 25.0 (IBM; Armonk, New York, USA).

Differences in demographic characteristics, such as age, sex, and educational background in participants will be determined using independent-samples t-tests.
For further information about the behavioral analyses, you can consult the analysis plan described in the previous registration (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/QDEVJ).

Intra-brain activity analysis and seed region selection:
We will examine brain responses to task conditions in a classical general linear convolution model (GLM) and independent component analysis (ICA) to select regions of interest and extract time series for subsequent connectivity analysis. ICA is a data-driven blind source separation approach, which extracts the underlying, maximally independent sources (components) from a multivariate data set. By analyzing fMRI data in a model-free and hypothesis-free manner, the nonlinear and unpredictable dynamic of social interactions can be more appropriately captured.

Our plan is to use both theoretical regions of interest to start our analyses, as well as the brain regions we obtain with ICA. The reasoning behind this is that, although there is similar literature that can guide us about which brain areas to look at, as the study tasks have not been used previously in MRI, we cannot be sure that we are looking at the relevant areas. Thus, we aim to identify these areas first in a data driven approach.
In the same direction of reasoning, we have selected different methods of analysis that we could use depending on the data, we will be dealing with, and whether it is possible to use such a model.

The possible analysis approaches are:
1. Interpersonal brain-behavior dependencies (iBBDs): Capturing the brain responses of one individual which are modulated by, or depend on, the behavior of an interaction partner iBBDs model was created. In this model, brain signals that are elicited as a direct response to their interaction partner’s previous behavior are identified by an event-related model of each individual’s brain activity in a short period following each of their partner’s movements. For previous application in fMRI hyperscanning, see Špiláková, Shaw, Czekóová, & Brázdil, (2019).
2. Inter-subject correlation (ISC) analysis: ISC analyses are carried out to investigate whether the time-course of brain signals within these patterns are correlated or aligned between interactive pairs. ISC can be quantified using Pearson’s correlation coefficients between the time series of a given ROI between the two subjects. For previous application in fMRI hyperscanning, see Špiláková, Shaw, Czekóová, Mareček, & Brázdil, (2020) and Xie et al., (2020)
3. Actor-partner Independence Model (APIM): This model is designed to measure interdependence within interpersonal relationships because takes into account interdependencies by measuring associations between scores within the dyad and assessing the extent to which each member of the dyad influences the responses of the other member. In this model, individual measures are treated as being nested within the dyad. For example, if sibling A shows higher dominant behavior (defined as holding longer without turning) in the previous trial, this may influence his/ her next decision (actor effect) and the other’s decision (partner effect). We can include brain synchronization in this model by defining it as a possible moderator of the actor or partner effects. We will perform all tests using structural equation modeling and multilevel modeling. For further information, see Kashy & Kenny, 1999; Kenny, 1996, Fitzpatrick, Gareau, Lafontaine, & Gaudreau, 2016.
4. Dynamical causal modeling (DCM): In this model, instead of using BOLD responses, the effects of the level of the neural population are used. The effective connectivity (instead of the correlation between time series) is examined, as well as the direction of this connectivity between those brain regions. For each pair, a DCM model is specified taking ROIs as seed regions. For previous application in fMRI hyperscanning, see Bilek (2020).

We will use the following analysis time-windows:
CoTT:
All brain activity will be included for intra- and inter-brain analysis during the scenarios, separated by a waiting phase between mini-blocks.
ICG:
For the inter-brain activity analysis we will first look for synchronization in:
a) Decision-making during the driving phase (interactive car game).
b) Decision-making as a combination between the intuition question phase and driving phase.
iTAP:
We will separately analyze synchronization in:
a) Aggressive behavior: The money decision & provocation feedback.
b) Mentalizing behavior: rock-paper-scissors decision & outcome feedback.
For all the analysis approaches, we will use permutation tests to compare really interacting pairs to those of randomly composed non-pairs. Fake pairs are created by matching individuals from one pair with those who have performed the same task (and with the same and the opposite role, if possible). For example, by matching one person with the rotation role of pair A, and one person with the movement role of pair B). With these analyses, we ensure that the results are due to the real interaction. 61517817ec788500a640f925 Analysis plan.PNG https://osf.io/project/5jbk8/files/osfstorage/61517817ec788500a640f925 https://osf.io/download/61517817ec788500a640f925 189c34b71a76f8e63a97f3cf4e26248727e88a1344d47bff7f22e903af2fc3a4
transformations fMRI: After removal of the first three fMRI volumes, functional scans are realigned to the first volume of the remaining, co-registered to the T1 image, normalized to a standard template (MNI), and spatially smoothed with an 8×8×8 mm full-width at half-maximum Gaussian kernel. A high-pass filter with a cut-off of 128s is applied.
inference_criteria We will use the standard p<0.05 criteria for determining if t-test or ANOVA results are significantly different from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct. All second-level statistics are corrected for multiple comparisons with an extent family-wise error (FWE) corrected cluster level threshold at p<0.05 (a voxel-wise threshold at uncorrected p<0.001).
data_exclusion_criteria If a participant does not respond to any of the trials, the participant will be excluded.
missing_data_handling If a participant does not respond to any of the trials, the participant will be excluded.
exploratory_analyses We will calculate the correlation between the team performance and the degree of observed INS across participants within each pair. Finally, we will do some exploratory correlation analyses between behavioral measures (e.g. average aggression), questionnaires data (e.g. AQ total score), and selected brain regions (e.g. PFC).
Outcome variables of the three tasks may also be related to each other.
additional_comments The pre-registration of the pilot study of this project can be found here: https://osf.io/qdevj/?view_only=95c3afba2b7e4de0a63edbc534c5e44d

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform.
